sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
June 2026 delivered a mixed global equity tape defined by three competing forces: a historic collapse in crude oil prices following the U.S.–Iran ceasefire framework, a hawkish Federal Reserve surprise under Chair Kevin Warsh that reset the U.S. rates outlook, and the record-breaking SpaceX IPO that underscored extraordinary capital-markets depth. The S&P 500 recorded its first losing month after back-to-back gains in April and May, closing at **7,499.36** — down **-1.0%** for June — while the Dow Jones Industrial Average set a new all-time record at **52,319.20** and the Nasdaq Composite finished at **26,213.72**.

Despite June's softness, H1 2026 performance was exceptional: the S&P 500 advanced **+9.6%** for the half-year, the Nasdaq delivered **+12.8%**, and Q2 alone posted a **+15.2%** S&P gain — the best quarterly performance in six years. In APAC, the Nikkei 225 remained the standout global index, notching its third consecutive monthly record and closing June at approximately **70,062** after breaching **72,300** intraday — a new all-time high — on AI and semiconductor exuberance. European indices surrendered ground across the board, with the DAX, CAC 40, and FTSE 100 all declining under the combined pressure of dollar strength and energy-sector earnings downgrades.

The month's defining macro dynamic was the resolution of the U.S.–Iran Strait of Hormuz crisis, which sent Brent crude plunging **-22.9%** — one of the sharpest monthly oil declines in a generation — relieving stagflationary pressure across equity and credit markets simultaneously. The juxtaposition of collapsing energy prices and a hawkish Fed pivot created a complex cross-asset environment, rewarding selectivity and sector rotation over passive concentration in mega-cap technology.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
SpaceX IPO Redefines Capital Markets Scale -- The singular capital markets event of June 2026 was the June 12 listing of SpaceX (ticker: SPCX) on the Nasdaq, marking the largest initial public offering in history. The company priced at **$135** per share, raising approximately **$75 billion** and implying a valuation of approximately **$1.8 trillion** at listing; the stock opened at **$150** and closed its first trading session at **$160.95** — a **+19%** first-day gain — pushing the implied market capitalization above **$2 trillion** and briefly making Elon Musk the first individual to hold more than a trillion dollars in listed equity value.

The SpaceX debut was the headline event in an extraordinary first-half for U.S. equity capital markets, with Alphabet concurrently raising **$85 billion** in a landmark secondary equity offering and total H1 2026 U.S. IPO and secondary issuance topping a new half-year record. The depth of institutional and retail absorption of this historic supply without material index-level disruption underscored the extraordinary risk appetite and balance-sheet strength that characterized the 2026 bull market cycle.

For portfolio allocators, SPCX introduces a formidable new benchmark for capital within the technology and aerospace theme. With several additional large-cap unicorns reportedly preparing H2 filings, the net supply of public equity is likely to accelerate — a dynamic that must be incorporated into H2 positioning alongside an already elevated valuations environment.

US–Iran Ceasefire Triggers Historic Oil Price Collapse -- The most consequential commodity market dislocation in a generation partially unwound in June, as Washington and Tehran reached a framework ceasefire agreement reopening the Strait of Hormuz — a waterway handling roughly 20% of global crude supply — to all international shipping. The IEA had estimated the Strait's closure was creating a daily global supply shortfall of **14 million barrels**, a shock without modern precedent that had driven Brent crude to an all-time high of **$138.21/bbl** in early April.

Brent crude plunged **-22.9%** in June to close at **$71.59/bbl** — its lowest level since before the conflict began — as Iran's oil sanctions relief was structured to take effect immediately upon signing. WTI fell a parallel **-21.2%** to **$71.87/bbl**. The EIA revised its outlook significantly lower, and Goldman Sachs cut its Q4 2026 Brent forecast to **$80/bbl** from a prior **$90/bbl**, reflecting expectations that Iranian barrels would gradually re-enter the global supply pool over H2 2026.

For equities, the ceasefire was a material tailwind — removing the stagflationary impulse that had weighed on risk assets — but the implications for energy-sector earnings in H2 2026 are considerably more challenging. E&P companies now face a structurally lower commodity price than consensus had assumed weeks earlier, and guidance revisions represent a likely source of earnings drag for the second half of the year.

Warsh's Hawkish Fed Pivot Reshapes the U.S. Rates Outlook -- Kevin Warsh's inaugural FOMC meeting as Federal Reserve Chair delivered a hawkish shock that upended the consensus view that a Trump-backed central banker would tilt dovish. The committee held the policy rate steady at **3.50%–3.75%** but removed key forward-guidance language signaling a future easing bias; nine of 18 FOMC participants now project at least one rate hike before year-end 2026, with six projecting two or more — a dot-plot configuration that was materially more hawkish than pre-meeting market pricing.

The reaction across asset classes was swift: the 2-year Treasury yield surged more than **16 basis points** on the announcement day — the largest single-session move on a Fed decision day since March 2008 — the U.S. dollar accelerated with the DXY rising to approximately **103.99** (approx., verify before merging), a multi-month high, and USD/JPY climbed toward **160** (approx., verify before merging), raising the probability of Japanese Ministry of Finance intervention and triggering a significant unwind in yen-funded carry trades.

The macro implications are far-reaching: a rate-hike cycle restart — the first since 2022–2023 — was not discounted by equity or credit markets entering June. The resulting repricing of the risk-free rate introduced meaningful uncertainty into H2 2026 earnings multiple assumptions, with rate-sensitive sectors including real estate, utilities, and long-duration growth equities facing incremental headwinds, while the banking sector stands to benefit from wider net interest margins if the hiking cycle materializes.

Alphabet Joins the Dow and Market Leadership Broadens -- On June 29, Alphabet (GOOGL) replaced Verizon Communications in the Dow Jones Industrial Average in the most significant index reconstitution in years. S&P Dow Jones Indices cited Alphabet's differentiated exposure to artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, and digital advertising as the rationale for the change. Alphabet shares rallied **+3.7%** on debut day, pushing the Dow above **52,000** for the first time in its 130-year history and contributing to the index's closing record of **52,319.20** at June month-end.

Beyond the index optics, June saw a meaningful and potentially durable rotation in market leadership. Value beat growth decisively, healthcare posted its best monthly performance since November, industrials and financials outperformed, and equal-weight benchmarks significantly outpaced their cap-weighted counterparts. The U.S. flash composite PMI rose to **52.2** in June, with the manufacturing sub-index climbing to **55.7** — its highest reading since May 2022 — providing fundamental validation for the cyclical rotation narrative.

If the broadening beyond mega-cap technology that emerged in June is sustained through Q3 and Q4, it would represent a critical evolution of the current bull market: from a narrow, AI-concentration-driven advance into a broad-based expansion of earnings growth. This scenario has material implications for active management alpha, sector allocation, and the relative attractiveness of mid- and small-cap equities versus the mega-cap names that have dominated since 2024.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
U.S. equity markets posted a measured setback in June, with the S&P 500 declining **-1.0%** to close at **7,499.36** — its first losing month after back-to-back gains of **+10.5%** in April and **+5.3%** in May. The retreat was orderly rather than disorderly, driven primarily by a hawkish repricing of the Federal Reserve's policy trajectory following Chair Warsh's inaugural FOMC meeting, which compressed multiples in rate-sensitive and longer-duration growth equities while pushing Treasury yields and the dollar sharply higher. Despite June's softness, H1 2026 performance remained exceptional: the S&P 500 advanced **+9.6%** and the Nasdaq **+12.8%** for the half-year, and Q2 posted a **+15.2%** gain — the best quarter in six years.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at **26,213.72** at month-end, with semiconductor names coming under notable pressure through the back half of June after their extraordinary prior-quarter run. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was the relative standout, setting a new all-time record at **52,319.20**, powered by the landmark addition of Alphabet on June 29 as a member of the blue-chip index; Alphabet rallied **+3.7%** on its Dow debut day, driving the index above **52,000** for the first time in its history.

Beneath the headline indices, June's most consequential development was the broadening of market leadership. Healthcare, financials, and industrials outperformed; equal-weight benchmarks significantly outpaced cap-weighted equivalents; and value trounced growth. The month also featured a record-setting equity issuance calendar — anchored by SpaceX's **$75 billion** IPO on June 12 at **$135** per share, with the stock closing its first session at **$160.95** — signaling both exceptional corporate confidence and deep market liquidity.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets gave back ground across the board in June, with the DAX declining approximately **-1.5%** (approx., verify before merging), the CAC 40 losing approximately **-2.0%** (approx., verify before merging), and the FTSE 100 falling approximately **-1.7%** (approx., verify before merging). All three indices were pressured by a combination of dollar strength, resurgent ECB rate-tightening expectations, and the structural disadvantage of a region with limited AI and semiconductor exposure relative to the U.S. and Japan. The ECB's June decision — which held rates while signaling a more cautious posture on future easing — reinforced concerns that European monetary conditions would remain tighter for longer.

The collapse in crude oil prices following the U.S.–Iran ceasefire offered a partial offset for energy-importing European economies, with airlines, logistics, and consumer discretionary names catching a bid on lower input-cost expectations. However, FTSE 100 and European energy producers gave back significant ground as Brent fell to **$71.59/bbl**, threatening fiscal break-evens and dividend coverage ratios in energy names that had been key index constituents. The eurozone composite PMI remained above 50, indicating ongoing expansion, but the narrative was overshadowed by dollar-strength headwinds and the potential ripple effects of the Warsh Fed's hawkish pivot on global financial conditions.

The relative underperformance of European equities versus the U.S. in June extends a year-to-date pattern. With the ECB holding and the Fed now signaling potential hikes, the rate-differential dynamic is shifting in ways that may attract incremental capital toward dollar-denominated assets at the expense of European ones. Q2 earnings season will be closely watched for signs that European corporate margins can absorb higher financing costs and weaker Chinese demand — two of the defining challenges facing the region's export-oriented economy heading into H2 2026.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets delivered a sharply bifurcated outcome in June, with Japan's Nikkei 225 notching its third consecutive monthly record on continued AI and semiconductor investment tailwinds, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index underperformed materially, declining approximately **-5%** to close near **22,671** — weighed by softer consumer internet sentiment, persistent weakness in property and financial-sector stocks, and residual uncertainty about Chinese domestic demand. The divergence between Tokyo's strength and Hong Kong's weakness crystallized the defining regional investment theme of 2026: a decisive global preference for AI infrastructure and semiconductor exposure over traditional consumer internet platforms.

The Nikkei 225 was the standout global index of the month, breaking the **68,000** level for the first time on June 3 and reaching an intra-month high above **72,300** before closing June at approximately **70,062** — a monthly gain of approximately **3,732 points**. The advance reflected structural enthusiasm for Japan's semiconductor supply-chain buildout, yen-weakness-driven earnings tailwinds for exporters, and sustained foreign institutional inflows into Japanese equities as a global AI-capex proxy. Concerns about AI overinvestment and profit-taking in semiconductor names triggered bouts of volatility toward month-end, capping the index's gains. China's Shanghai Composite posted a modest gain to close at approximately **4,094** (approx., verify before merging), with moves concentrated in targeted policy-support sectors.

Structurally, China's equity market continues to trade in a constrained range, with policymakers balancing targeted demand-side stimulus against persistent property-sector headwinds and geopolitical trade uncertainty. The People's Bank of China held policy rates steady through June, keeping its powder dry as it assessed the impact of the U.S.–Iran resolution on global commodity prices and trade flows. For APAC allocators, the key question entering H2 2026 is whether Chinese policy stimulus will be sufficient to close the performance gap with the region's AI-driven outperformers, or whether the Nikkei versus Hang Seng divergence will widen further.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The U.S. dollar dominated the June FX tape, with the DXY index advancing sharply to close near **103.99** (approx., verify before merging) — building on May's gains and marking the broadest G10 dollar advance in more than a year. The primary catalyst was the hawkish pivot from the Warsh-led Federal Reserve, which widened the U.S. rate differential decisively in the dollar's favor: the 2-year Treasury yield advanced more than **16 basis points** on the FOMC day alone, while yields in the eurozone, UK, and Japan either held steady or declined, amplifying the carry advantage of long-USD positions.

EUR/USD declined into the **1.14–1.15** range (approx., verify before merging) as ECB rate-hike expectations faded and eurozone growth signals remained uneven. GBP/USD held relatively better, settling near **1.34**, supported by sticky UK services inflation and Bank of England pricing that kept residual hike probabilities alive. USD/JPY was the focal cross of the month, surging toward **160** (approx., verify before merging) — revisiting levels that previously triggered Ministry of Finance intervention — as the Bank of Japan maintained its accommodative stance against the backdrop of rising U.S. yields, pushing the pair toward discomfort thresholds.

The broader FX takeaway from June is a decisive re-rating of U.S. monetary exceptionalism under Chair Warsh. Markets that entered the month pricing in an eventual easing pivot were badly wrong-footed, with the hawkish recalibration repricing the dollar sharply higher across the board. The strategic risk entering H2 2026 is twofold: the potential for disorderly yen depreciation that forces Japanese authorities to intervene — disrupting global carry-trade dynamics — and an emerging-market FX channel where a stronger dollar tightens financial conditions for dollar-denominated borrowers across Asia and Latin America.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Crude oil was the defining commodity story of June by a wide margin, with both benchmarks posting one of the sharpest monthly declines in a generation following the U.S.–Iran framework peace agreement. Brent crude — which had surged to an all-time high of **$138.21/bbl** in early April on the Strait of Hormuz closure — averaged **$85/bbl** in June (down **$22/bbl** from May's average of **$107/bbl**) and closed the month at **$71.59/bbl**, a monthly decline of **-22.9%**. WTI fell in parallel to **$71.87/bbl**, down **-21.2%** for June. Goldman Sachs revised its Q4 2026 Brent forecast to **$80/bbl** from a prior **$90/bbl**, reflecting expectations that Iranian barrels would gradually re-enter the global supply pool over H2.

Gold retreated from earlier highs, settling near **$4,062/oz** (approx., verify before merging) at month-end as the safe-haven bid unwound alongside reduced geopolitical risk premium from the Iran ceasefire, and rising real U.S. yields — a byproduct of the Warsh Fed's hawkish pivot — capped the metal's upside. Central bank demand and residual geopolitical uncertainty continue to provide structural support, but the near-term risk-reward for gold shifted less favorable as the Iran crisis discount unwound and dollar strength created an additional headwind for the non-yielding metal.

Copper was the notable outperformer across the broader commodity complex, remaining close to multi-year highs near approximately **$6.39/lb** (approx., verify before merging), driven by robust Chinese import volumes, rising speculative long positioning, and structural supply constraints in the global copper mining pipeline. The divergence between collapsing crude and resilient copper captures a key commodity market message: the energy supply shock was idiosyncratic and politically resolvable, while the structural demand for industrial metals tied to electrification and AI infrastructure buildout remains intact and demand-inelastic.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
U.S. Treasury markets experienced one of their most consequential single-meeting repricings in years in June, as the Warsh-led FOMC delivered a hawkish shock that sent the 2-year Treasury yield surging more than **16 basis points** on the announcement day — the largest single-session move on a Fed decision day since March 2008. The Fed held the federal funds rate steady at **3.50%–3.75%** but removed key policy-statement language signaling a future easing bias; nine of 18 FOMC members now project at least one rate hike before year-end 2026, with six projecting two or more — a dot-plot configuration materially more hawkish than pre-meeting market pricing.

The 10-year Treasury yield settled at **4.38%** at June month-end, while the 2-year yield reached **4.07%**, maintaining a positively sloped yield curve with a spread of approximately **+31 basis points**. The positive curve slope marked a meaningful contrast to the deeply inverted readings that defined the 2023–2024 period and represents a tentative normalization of the term structure. The near-term risk is that further hawkish signaling re-inverts the curve if short-end yields reprice more aggressively than the long end as markets price in additional hike probability.

Corporate bonds remained broadly resilient despite the rates shock, with investment-grade spreads holding contained even as high-yield saw modest widening in credit-sensitive sectors. Global sovereign bonds outside the U.S. posted modest gains as yields in the eurozone, UK, and Japan held steady or declined — a divergence that amplified dollar strength and set up a more complex global rates landscape for H2 2026. With nine FOMC members projecting at least one hike, fixed income volatility is likely to remain elevated, and duration positioning represents a key risk factor for cross-asset portfolios entering the second half of the year.
